#9877. AI made self-hosting fun again

Jan-Lukas ElseTech, life and everything else

I’ve been self-hosting things for many years. There were times when I was quite enthusiastic about it, constantly trying out new software and tinkering with my infrastructure. But at some point, that enthusiasm faded a bit.I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me.Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that.Less frictionMost of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project.Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort.In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.Trying things I always found interestingThere are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me.Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that.Less frictionMost of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project.Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort.In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.Trying things I always found interestingThere are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.Trying things I always found interestingThere are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

A monthly overview of things you need to know as an architect or aspiring architect.

QCon AI New York (December 15-16, 2026): Learn how senior engineers are building AI systems that hold up in production. Register Now

Facilitating the Spread of Knowledge and Innovation in Professional Software Development

Unlock the full InfoQ experience by logging in! Stay updated with your favorite authors and topics, engage with content, and download exclusive resources.

In this episode, Christopher "CRob" Robinson, CTO of OpenSSF, Akrites, and chief security architect of the Linux Foundation, explores the state of software supply chain security amid multiple security incidents and explains how tools like Scorecard, the Security Baseline framework, and SLSA help harden software.

Saranya Vedagiri explains how to design resilient, low-latency distributed APIs under 100ms. Drawing on practical scale at eBay, she discusses hop-by-hop latency budgets, async fanout tradeoffs, thread pool sizing, caching, and circuit breakers. Learn actionable strategies to eliminate tail-latency bottlenecks and establish performance-first engineering practices.

Rachel Shalom explains how Dell solved enterprise RAG retrieval failures on internal terminology by fine-tuning open-source embedding models. She discusses data prep with hard negatives, distributed InfoNCE loss training on H100 GPUs, automated hyperparameter tuning, and production evaluation using LLM-as-a-judge.

Laura Savino discusses the psychological friction of AI adoption for senior engineers & architects. She explains how shifting from static expertise to learning in public lowers anxiety, accelerates tooling fluency, and prevents burnout. Leaders will discover actionable strategies to support their teams, debunk tech zealotry, and foster an adaptive engineering culture that thrives during upheaval.

The panelists explore how engineering teams adapt delivery architectures, pipelines, security, and governance for AI-assisted development. They share practical strategies for verifying AI-generated code, solving testing and deployment bottlenecks, maintaining human oversight, and measuring AI’s true impact on software velocity, quality, reliability, and operational cost.

Work through your production AI decisions with senior engineers from other companies. Apply their perspectives to challenges from your own work.Online. Register Now.

Compare team design, delivery flow, AI roles, and metrics with experienced practitioners. Online. Register Now.

Building RAG pipelines or AI agents? Work through retrieval, context, evals, and reliability decisions with experienced practitioners.Online. Register Now.

Distributed systems, decentralized decisions, platform engineering, and AI architecture. Online. Register Now.

Production AI across agents, context, evals, security, and infrastructure, from the senior engineers building it.Register. Early bird ends Dec 10.

What early-adopter teams have proven in production, across 15 engineering tracks. Register. Early bird ends Dec 10.

Learn from the decisions and trade-offs behind AI systems already running in production.Register. Early bird ends Jan 12.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Finetuning Your Embedding Model for Better Search: Learning from Agentic Search at Dell

Rachel Shalom explains how Dell solved enterprise RAG retrieval failures on internal terminology by fine-tuning open-source embedding models. She discusses data prep with hard negatives, distributed InfoNCE loss training on H100 GPUs, automated hyperparameter tuning, and production evaluation using LLM-as-a-judge.

Rachel Shalom is an applied AI scientist and Distinguished Engineer with 7+ years of experience turning cutting edge AI into real world impact. She specializes in LLM-based knowledge retrieval, multi-agent systems, and deep learning for time series data, building solutions that don’t just work, they get used.

QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

Rachel Shalom: I'm Rachel. I work for Dell. I'm part of a team that develops internal AI solutions for Dell. We develop solutions that basically Dell employees are using. I'm going to talk about some of the work we are doing inside Dell today. I'm actually going to start with the motivation of this talk. I'm leading an agentic search within Dell, a search system that searches for your information in internal sources like GitHub, Jira, Confluence, and other sources. Part of it is using semantic search, which is using also an embedding model. What we have noticed is that we keep failing in certain type of questions. Questions that have to do with internal terminology or questions that have to do with internal products of Dell. Here are some examples like PowerScale or CloudIQ or PowerProtect. These are the type of questions that are using internal terminology, or you can call it even internal language of Dell, that the system kept failing with retrieving the right answer. The motivation was, does the embedding model that is supposed to capture the meaning of those really understand the questions or the answers?

This is what we are going to talk about today. We'll discuss why embedding models are important and common training methodologies. We'll discuss also the common use cases for embeddings. I will talk about fine-tuning and a common loss function that is used today for training majority of the embedding models. We will talk about the use case at Dell more in depth and why we trained our own embedding model, discuss the data collection, and how did we evaluate and monitor the performance.

Humans understand words, machines understand numbers. Embeddings is the bridge between them. Embedding is capturing the meaning of words and sentences. For example, you can see in that lane that in the embedding space, expressions that have to do with password or forgot my login or can't access account should be closer in the embedding space, while cities and countries will be in a different area in the embedding space, but closer to each other, and that's the meaning of representations. What are the common use cases for using embedding models? I think the most common one is information retrieval. Most of the companies or at least in the enterprise, you use RAG, Retrieval-Augmented Generation to retrieve information from a vector database. Classification is one more. For example, if you want to assign categories to your text, like you have incoming emails, the most trivial example is you want to target spam or not spam. Clustering is another very common use case for embedding models. If you want to make sense of your unstructured data, like you have incoming queries by customers and you want to group them together into clusters and recommendation systems to make personalized recommendations. There are probably others, but these are the most common ones.

Now I want to talk briefly on the general training procedures for embedding models. Usually when you train embedding models, you start with the first phase, which is the pre-training. Pre-training is done on what we call the chunk of the internet. You take everything that is available online, Wikipedia, books, public GitHub repository, anything you can imagine, and it's a lot of data, and it can be also junk data, but it's a lot of data that you put in. The way you train is by Masked Language Modeling, which means, as you see in the example, is that you give the model a sentence, each time you mask a different word, and then you let the model guess the word, and this is how you teach the model a general understanding of the language. A little bit of grammar, a little bit of word connections, but a very general understanding, not the fine-grained understanding of semantic meaning of each word, and for that, you have stage number two, which is a fine-tuning stage.

At this stage, you really have to collect high-quality data. Usually it takes a long time, and it costs a lot of money normally. I'm going to talk about the preparation of what we call contrastive learning, which is a very common way to train or fine-tune embedding models nowadays. What you do normally is you prepare pairs or triplets of examples. For example, here, you have a question. Let's call it an anchor. How do I reset my password? Then you have a positive answer, which is how to reset it, and then you have a negative answer, which doesn't answer your question. The idea in training is that you want to teach the model that the question and the positive answer will be represented as vectors that are very close in the embedding space, and the negative answer and the anchor are going to be further apart. That's the goal of the fine-tuning, to take high-quality data and get the real semantic meaning for the text.

How do you do that? I'm putting here a little bit of mathematics, and I'm going to explain each part of it. I think it's beautiful, and this is important that you will see it. InfoNCE, or the long-term in parentheses, loss function is one of the most common ones. If you take a look at different papers from Google or anyone else that is training embedding models, you will see different versions of the same loss function, but this is the basic one. If we go and see the batch, or we have let's say 100 examples of questions and answers, so if we take a look at a log expression, you will see that on the top we have the exponent of s is a cosine similarity between two vectors, the vector of the question and the vector of the positive answer. On the denominator, you're going to see again the similarity of the question and the positives, and the similarity of the question and negatives.

All other documents that are not the positive one to this question are considered negatives, because they are not directly answering the question. When you train an embedding model, the purpose is to bring up the similarity for positives and bring down the similarity for negatives. I added another slide for that just to maybe show it in a geometric way, so that you don't lose the context. Again, we have this log loss of positives versus negatives. If we take a look at the lower part, then you can see that if I have, let's say, a query, how do I reset my password? Then I have a positive question and a bunch of negative questions. Then, before training, you will see that the distance between the positive and negative vectors to the query are maybe, let's say, a little bit similar, and after training, you want to see that the positive answer is closer to the query, and the negatives are further away. I hope you at least enjoyed a little bit from this loss function. It's super beautiful.

Another thing that is interesting about the training is what we call prefix use. What does that mean? Sometimes we have what we call conflicting reward signals. Think about a model that is performing different tasks. Sometimes it is questions and answers. Sometimes it is clustering, as we mentioned before. Sometimes it is other tasks. Then if we take a look at this example, what is the capital of France? I want you to answer what is mostly similar, answer number one or answer number two. I think the answer would be it depends on the task. If we want to do clustering similarity between two sentences, then what is the capital of France, and number one would be more similar. If my task is to pair questions and answers, then what is the capital of France, and number two is more similar. In order to solve that, what is commonly done today when training with fine-tuning is to add prefixes.

As you can see, we have in orange the start clustering, what is the capital of France, and then clustering the answer, and that tells the model, please create vectors for clustering. They're going to get slightly different vectors because the task now is to say, these are two similar sentences. If I provide a different prefix, which is search_query, search_document, so the task is questions and answers. This is where you give the model a signal that we are now talking about a different task. This is one important thing to notice when training.

I've talked a little bit about the use cases and a little bit generally about the training. Now let's talk about Dell, or what we did at Dell. We have an agentic search at Dell, which means we let R&D teams search within all of Dell's internal sources. For example, Jira, Confluence, GitHub, these are mostly relevant for engineers and product managers, SharePoint, also different databases. I'm going to talk about the architecture, but this is a hierarchical architecture of multiple agents that are making API calls. It also has a component of semantic search, which means we take all the data and ingest it in advance. It has a component of memory management, which is pretty common for agentic search applications. It's also permission aware, which is very important for any enterprise. These are some of the questions that we are getting normally, questions about bug solving, questions about onboarding to a new project, testing, technical configurations, procedural how-to.

We get all sorts of also weird questions, but these are the most common ones. This is a little bit on the architecture of the system itself. We have the orchestrator, or what we call the supervisor, which is the entry point for every question. This is a router that routes the user question to any other of the agents. We have a GitHub agent, which means that it's a model with a set of tools, mainly API tools. We have a Confluence agent that is a model. They all have access, or it's access-based, to the information inside Dell. We have GitLab and GitHub, which is, again, exactly the same. Models with different API tools. We have security agent, which usually makes API calls to OSs like Ubuntu and SUSE, and provide CVE resolutions, and agents that are making database queries. Just to note that each one of these agents are talking only to the supervisor.

We keep them that way in order to keep the context low and the context in place. We found it more effective that way. The supervisors can route the question to one or many agents. They return back an answer. The supervisor decides, do I want to go back to the user with an answer, or go back to the agents and bring another one? We, of course, limit the number of turns, so it won't take like one hour to get back to the user. This is how it works.

That is when someone wants to create their own bot, let's say, you just provide, here is a link to my Confluence or to my Jira, to my GitHub, and then it triggers a pipeline that does a lot of data plumbing, and ingest and chunk all the data, put it in a vector database, and it's ready for you to query. You can create your personal context space. A little bit more about the bring your own data architecture, it's important because this is the part that connects later to our embedding model, which is the main subject. If you have Jira, Confluence, and GitHub, we're taking all of the fields from Confluence, we take all the images and attachments, and so is for Jira. We do semantic chunks with code. We use AST, and we do a lot of cleanups, like these are too many details to talk about.

Then you might ask yourself, ok, so you do all of that job, but the rate of change is very high, so we update it every two days. We go and check with the APIs what were the changes, and then we re-embed all the changes every two days. Everything is saved in pgvector, which is, again, hosted on-prem, which I think is very nice that everything is hosted on-prem at Dell, that it's all private, nothing goes out. Just a little bit about chunking. I'm talking only on Confluence now because the work that we did in training the model, the context was Confluence. We start with an API fetch, or think about Confluence space, if you work with Confluence, you download thousands of pages, then we reformat it into HTML. We filter a lot of noise because there are a lot of emojis and stuff that are not relevant to the model, we turn it into an md file. We detect also tables to make sure that the context of the table is saved even when you chunk. We take all those attachments and then we chunk by paragraphs and use an embedding model and save it in a vector database. This is done for every request that we get and in advance.

Now the question is, ok, so we have a system in place, we have lots of agents and we have also semantic search, now why fine-tune our own embedding? I started the lecture with saying that we saw gaps that the semantic search just didn't solve, and the gaps were mainly about questions on internal products, on abbreviations and acronyms that are specific to Dell, and workflows and processes, everything that is the Dell world or the Dell language, there are a lot of such data at Dell, that led us to think or to hypothesize that this is a reason for failure. Now when you run a RAG system, so there are potentially a lot of problems that could happen. It has a lot of stages and a lot of pieces moving around, so it could be something else. Our hypothesis said, let's try and see if we can improve the result by fine-tuning a model.

Generally speaking, I think that the signals you want to look for if you are planning a domain adaptation are to ask yourself like, is the data of the model out of the shelf that I'm taking on? Now I'm talking about models in the context of open source. We take most of the models from Hugging Face, normally you know what is the training data that they were trained on, you have leaderboards. You ask yourself, is the Dell data even similar to what those models were trained on? It can be that the terminology we use was used when this model was trained originally. These are the signs to look for when you want to train. There is another interesting thing to check. Again, every open-source model comes with a vocabulary. It's a list of tokens that the model has seen. This one was around 30,000. What happens when the model hasn't seen that word, they have a special token called unknown token.

That means the model said, I haven't seen that but I can manage, never mind. I put an unknown token. I wanted to understand how many unknown tokens do we have that the model completely hasn't seen at all? Not that it doesn't understand the semantics, it just didn't see those words. I was surprised to see that these are very general. I put here some examples that I saw, like Base64-encoded strings, or you can see Unicode box-drawing, all of these things that really have no meaning. It makes sense. All of the images, the model didn't recognize, that was surprising. I thought that models are trained on images now. Checkmarks and long camelCase compound words. This was a very small percentage of the data that the model didn't recognize. The reason I checked it is because when you fine-tune a model, I would like the model to semantically understand my data. If most of the tokens that I have in my data do not exist in the model vocabulary, that's a reason to start training from scratch, not fine-tuning. That was a check. The check told me, it's fine. The model doesn't understand images. I don't care. Let's move on. We are continuing with fine-tuning.

There is also the inference cost and latency. How fast is this model? Does it support multilingual and not only English? Lastly, the context length. How much text can I push in at once? Then we ended up at comparing two, EmbeddingGemma and Nomic Embed, mainly because we were very limited in the licensing part. Just a funny story, before we used those, we used the BGE family. These are Chinese family. Then for some reason, Chinese models were banned from some American companies. Then we had to redo the whole work with models that are allowed. Both of them have great licenses. They are both open, even though I must say that comparing to Google, Nomic Embed by Nomic, they released it all. You are welcome to go and try. They released the training code, the model, the data. Anyone can reproduce the work. It's amazing. In terms of parameters or size, both of them are tiny, so it's great.

They are really fast. Context length, you can see that Google contains only 2K and Nomic Embed contains 8K. Google supports multilingual. If I go to best fit, then we decided, I have a choice now between Confluence, GitHub, and Jira. Now when we took a look at Google, they were very optimized for code search. We chose the EmbeddingGemma for code embedding. For Confluence, we decided we go with Nomic Embed because it has extensive technical documents it was trained on. Also, the context length gives us more flexibility when we want to embed things from Confluence.

Going back to Confluence, I want to talk a little bit about, we decided now to fine-tune, now how do you start. You need to start preparing data, that's the hardest part, harder than just fine-tuning. We started with taking chunks, and I'm going to provide examples in the next slide. The chunking part, we did already in advance, so it was easy just to take the chunks we already handled. Then, step two, once I have one chunk, let's say, I'm taking an LLM to help me generate questions for that chunk. We generated three questions for each chunk, and of course, you can play with the number, that the chunks are supposed to answer those questions. This is how you generate, as you remember, the question and the positive document. Now, I would like to generate the negative documents. How do I do that? I have the questions, so we did a trick, and we took each question, and we went to the vector database, and we say, ok, let's take a model that wasn't trained, and retrieve documents from our vector database, but just, let's cap it so that the similarity when we retrieve is larger than 30%, but less than 80%.

We keep it in a range where the answer probably is not the most exact answer, but are not very far away. It's what we call hard negatives. They are answers that are not exactly answering what you ask, but they're not very far away, and we want to distinguish between those. We took the top 20, once you have 20 for the training, we kept 7 out of them. The number of negatives per training is just a parameter, and you can decide what to do. Then, you create triplets out of this process. How do you create triplets? That was a description of the process, so it's important you see one example in front of you, so a passage. We have to install Windsurf on Ubuntu WSL, just install. This is a chunk that we have. Now, I need to generate three questions out of it with an LLM.

As you can see, I generated three questions that are in purple, and the answers in green are exactly this identical chunk. Now, I went to the database and I retrieved other chunks that are going to be the negative answers. In this process, I've created to myself three samples. Each sample contains one question, one answer, and one document that is positive documents, and then seven negative documents.

I wanted to take a look at the data to see and check two things. On the top, I wanted to check the number of tokens for each part. I wanted to see what is the distribution of tokens for the questions, and you see it's roughly between zero to 50. This is a sample. Then I wanted to see what is the token distribution for the positive answers, which are roughly up to 1,500. Then I wanted to see what is the distribution of the negative answer, which are the same, up to 1,000, but we add a little bit more. This is important because the model is limited by context, so you want to make sure that you don't have very large context. Second thing is the cosine similarity distribution. As you see below, I wanted to compare the distribution of the question and the positives, and the question of the negatives.

What would you expect it to be? In a perfect world, I would expect that the distribution of question and the positive document would be very high, and take it to the right, the green one should be on the right. The distribution of similarities between negatives and the question would be to the left, very low similarities. As you can see here, it's a start where they are pretty similar. My goal, or what I will check after I'm going to train, is if I manage to create that separation, meaning the similarities of positives are going to be on the right side, and similarities of negatives are going to be on the left side. One more thing about fine-tuning with Auto Research. Some of you have trained models in the past. You know that, at least in the past, it was babysitting the models. You have a lot of parameters to play with in the model, learning rate, batch size, whatever it is.

Every time, you do a round, you wait a few hours, and then you start with different parameters. I think a month ago, Andrej Karpathy released what they called Auto Research, and he said, I just created an md file. I told the model, it's an LLM training an LLM. That's what it is. I gave my Claude Code, I think it was Opus 4.6. I told it, here is a training loop, here is the configuration file. You are only allowed to play with the training code and the parameters and the configuration, nothing else. Don't stop until the human stops you. Just make experiments. Each experiment should last 10 minutes, and then check the loss. If the loss goes down, keep those parameters. Loss goes up, remove those parameters, and move on. I just let it run overnight, and it really did save me a lot of time, because I came up, I looked at the experiment he made. I must say that there were some stupid stuff he did, but I chose one of the experiments that I liked, and I set up the learning rate, and the batch size, and everything, to what just the model told me. It was a nice experiment, and I think it is saving time.

I wanted to tell you a little bit about the setup for training. First of all is, I ran on four H100 GPUs. After all, I work at Dell, they have a lot of infrastructure. The number of negatives is 7. I used batch size of 128, and remember, the training data was Confluence spaces of almost all Dell. I counted the tokens, it was around 9 billion tokens in total. Then I wanted just for us to talk, or have a pick on distributed training. Let's take a look at the first part. If I have four GPUs, and I say I have 128 batch size, what does it mean in terms of documents? It means that I have 128 queries, or questions, and then I have, for each one of them, one positive answer, seven negative answers. I ended up with 1,024 additional documents on each GPU. Each GPU is getting one model, and 1,024 documents plus 128 queries.

We go to stage two. We start with the forward path. We put in the text, and we get vectors. What is interesting with this forward path is that, first, it is done in batches. It is done in batches of 32 in order to minimize memory consumption, but also, it is done in a way, we don't save any gradients, or the computational graph, let's call it. If you use PyTorch, so when saving a computational graph, it means you save the whole million parameters model activations, and it takes a lot of memory. When you don't save it, reduces the memory. What do you end up with after you do the forward path? You end up with vector. You started with text, now you have vector. Each vector is a dimension of 768. If we have 128 questions, so only for those, you end up with a matrix of 128 over the dimension of the vector, 768.

This is only for the queries. What else do we have? We have all the documents. We have 1,024 documents that are converted now to vectors in the size dimension of 768. What happened next? You have the all-gather. Each GPU now is collecting all the information from other GPUs. Now each GPU holds 4,096 vectors in a dimension of 768. Now we want to compute the loss. Remember the loss that we presented in the past where we want to compute similarities between the questions and positive answers and negative answers. This is where it is done. What is interesting here is that each GPU is seeing one question, one positive answer, and all the rest are going to be the negatives. You are getting now 4,095 negatives to compare against one positive. Why is it good? Because this is a harder task when the model is training. If you manage to train the model well, this is going to be a high-quality model because the task was differentiating between one question and 4,095 negative answers. Eventually when we do loss backward, there is the GradCache and surrogate trick to reduce memory when you calculate gradients. After we calculate the gradients on each GPU, you average them and then you update the model weights and start all over again.

This was a little bit about the distributed training at a high level. Now I want to go back to my EDA before on similarities. Remember that we said that we have similarities, the green one is the similarities between positives and questions, red is negative and questions. I wanted to say that I want to separate between them. You see the distribution before training and after training. As you can see, after training, you can see better separation, which means that it gives me a good signal or it gives me a signal, ok, the training did something well. Because now I see a separation, I see that the similarities of the questions and positive answers are a little bit more to the right. The question and the negative answer are a little bit more to the left. Yes, it's not perfect, there is still an overlap, but it's better than what it was.

Said, ok, good signal, let's continue. What do we need to check now? Let's talk about the evaluation setup. We have gathered what we call a golden dataset of 300 SME-verified questions, answers, and sources. Sources are like, if I ask you, how do I get Windsurf access? Then you will get an answer, but you will also get the links for Confluence that provide this answer. What I wanted to check is the recall @k, meaning, basically the question is, when I retrieve now, do I have the right sources? Did I retrieve the right URLs or not? When I say recall @1 is when I retrieve from the vector database, then it's top 1. Recall @10, it's top 10, organized by similarity. What we discovered is that, yes, we managed to fetch more correct sources when using the new models. I checked, let's say, top one or top five, but in reality, when you do a search system, you don't take top three or top five.

You take like more top 20. This is just for comparison to understand, ok, did I manage to get more or did I not? It seems like I did manage, at least in 12%, to get more resources right. Then, what is more interesting is eventually we are talking about a system that will provide eventually an answer to the user. What I care about is, did we provide the right answer? We did it, again, on the benchmarks that we built, using LLM-as-a-judge. LLM-as-a-judge has different aspects. One of them is question to answer. I want to know, does the text directly address the question? A2A is answer to answer, meaning does the answer match the ground truth? Because I have the ground truth. Here we saw an increase of a little bit more than 4%. It seems like, I would call it a good improvement, yes? Not a great success, but a very good improvement.

We said, ok, let's deploy it. What do you do in order to monitor? You would fine-tune your model. You have now a new model, and you want to say, do I need to retrain? What do I do? The first thing we do is we check the rate of data change. If we are talking about Confluence, we can check within a month, how much did it change? Do we have 1 million new pages? This is already a reason to start retraining. Check for data drift. You can check the distribution of the training data and compare it to your production data. The last thing is we actually have signs from our systems. If people are using our web application, they have the ability to put thumbs up and thumbs down. Also, we check if they click on the actual sources we provide on the website. If they stop clicking, it gives us a bad sign.

I hope that you will take away the importance of embedding. I think it's a topic that is normally overlooked. People are talking about embedding, but they don't understand how beautiful it is. Also wanted to talk a little bit about when fine-tuning is needed, a peek into the data preparation we did there and how we train, and why is it important to monitor and evaluate.

Participant 1: Before and after fine-tuning, did you compare with providing the documents in the context? Without fine-tuning, did you use RAG approach by sending the related document to the model and getting the answers and comparing that with the fine-tuned embeddings?

Rachel Shalom: Yes. We have RAG. We are using RAG, but not only. Like, when the user is asking questions and we let the router decide, do we need RAG or do we need an API call itself? We did test only the RAG, and it's not exactly testing. We saw at the beginning that this RAG is failing. It's failing normally in specific areas when we have documents that are very specific to Dell, like product relationships and acronyms that are at Dell, this is where there were failures that we tested at the beginning. Again, when you have failures at RAG, and there are many, you ask yourself, ok, so it could be a problem of indexing, it could be a problem of the wrong chunking, there could be many things. This was one of the hypotheses, that it might be that the model doesn't understand the context, and we need to retrain.

Participant 2: You mentioned images as one of the data sources. I was wondering, how does the embedding for images happen at Dell? Are the images embedded as raw content, or do you have some kind of an OCR that describes the images as text, and then the embedding happens?

Rachel Shalom: You are asking about like images, or attachments, or whatever. For different components, we did different things. For images, we took a multi-modal model that described the image and converted it into text, and this is how we chunked and then embed. Same thing for tables, I think. We understand the table structure, and the table start and end. Think about, you have now a table with 200 lines, and very complex. Since we know the dimensions of the table, so when you chunk it, then we always put the name of the columns for each chunk, and we always have in the metadata that this is part of the same table. This is for tables. What else? Attachments. Attachments are PDFs, and PPTs, and all others are parsed and chunked as part of the chunking and embedding. After chunks, we embed it.

Participant 3: I have a question on fine-tuning. Why did you decide you have to find seven negatives, and how did you find those? Was it manual? Was it automated?

Rachel Shalom: How did I decide on seven negatives?

Participant 3: Yes, you mentioned that you have a question, you have one positive and up to seven negatives.

Rachel Shalom: The simple question is, I read the Nomic paper, and they used seven. I said, ok, they had a great success, so I'm going to take seven. That's the simple answer. The second answer is, I let Auto Research play also with the number of negatives, and see what happens to the loss. Auto Research reduced it to like zero or one, and then, your loss is amazing. I'm like, "Oh my God." I kept it seven, because I think I really carefully took a look at the paper, and I thought, ok, it makes sense. If we need to add more, we add more. I didn't plan to put less, because I think the more negatives you have, the better the training will be, but even more complex. I would retrain with different numbers in the next experiments. The basic answer is the paper.

Participant 4: Just to clarify, the fine-tuning workflow that you showed us was for an internal workflow at Dell.

Rachel Shalom: For internal data, you mean?

Participant 4: Or like, the embedding model is an internal embedding model.

Rachel Shalom: The embedding model is open source. It's called Nomic Embed. You can download it from Hugging Face. They released it together with the code, even. They have a bunch of beautiful code to train for different tasks, and the training data. I didn't use, obviously, the training data, but it's running on-prem at Dell. I didn't use any API, if that's what you're asking, to train it. Completely on-prem. I downloaded the model to Dell infrastructure and trained it there.

Participant 4: I was just wondering if you've benchmarked it with some other open-source models that are out there?

Rachel Shalom: If I was experimenting with others?

Participant 4: Yes, just like OpenAI text embeddings, or anything like that?

Rachel Shalom: The reason I didn't do it is because we are not allowed to send data to OpenAI.

#9874. UK privacy watchdog faces probe into its workplace culture

Independent review will examine leadership, accountability, and how staff concerns were handled before former commissioner John Edwards resigned

Karon Monaghan KC will examine whether the regulator's culture and governance allowed problems to develop or made concerns harder to raise.

Edwards quit in June after an independent workplace investigation found there was a "case to answer" over his behavior and that his conduct fell short of what was expected of a public official. He disagreed with some of its findings, but ultimately conceded that he had shown "poor judgment."

That investigation, however, focused on Edwards alone. According to the terms of reference published on Thursday, it "did not consider the wider conditions in which that conduct occurred, and it was not designed to."

The new review will cast a wider net. Monaghan wants to know whether staff could call out bad behavior further up the food chain, and what awaited those who tried.

It will also poke around the regulator's leadership and governance arrangements and its relationship with its sponsoring government department, including whether there were adequate ways for concerns to be escalated and those at the top to be challenged.

Current and former staff can give evidence confidentially and voluntarily, while Monaghan will be given access to relevant documents and existing material, including staff surveys and data on bullying, harassment and discrimination.

The ICO has confirmed it won't use confidentiality clauses in settlement agreements to prevent people from contributing to the review.

Monaghan decides which witnesses and documents are relevant, rather than the ICO or DCMS. Access remains subject to legal restrictions, and she must be told when material is withheld and why. She can speak to whoever she thinks is relevant and ask for the complaints, correspondence, and other paperwork she needs.

And if that leads her somewhere unexpected, she can ask to widen the investigation. DCMS can refuse, but it won't be able to quietly brush the request aside, and any decision not to expand the scope has to make it into the final report.

The review won't reopen the investigation into Edwards, make findings about the conduct of named individuals, or delve into the merits of the regulator's enforcement decisions.

Its arrival comes amid a broader shake-up at Britain's data watchdog. The old Information Commissioner's Office was formally replaced by the Information Commission on September 30, bringing with it a new board-led governance model.

The government first promised the wider review in July, shortly after Edwards' departure, but it didn't appoint its reviewer or nail down the terms until late November.

"We need to understand what is working, where things are falling short and, crucially, what needs to change," said DCMS Secretary Lisa Nandy.

The watchdog won't have to wait long for its report card. Monaghan is expected to deliver her findings in the first quarter of 2027, after which they will be published and handed to Parliament. ®
